Deploy App is a tool to offer Software-as-a-Service to soldiers in a decentralized way. A Deploy App server gives a team a single, secure login and identity flow across a set of services they need.

Deploy App is build to be an integration target. It lets new services be added through integration APIs so users can onboard to them directly from the Deploy App UI.

What Deploy App is

Deploy App brings several services (chat, situational awareness, video, logging, and more) together behind one identity and one secure web UI. The design goals are explicit:

  • From zero to a running service with your team onboarded in about 30 minutes.
  • A fully reproducible deployment flow with no manual setup steps.
  • Security and quality first.

An operator stands up the stack, creates the first admin, invites and approves users, and those users then onboard to individual services (for example downloading a TAK client package) from the Deploy App home page.

An old internal name for Deploy App is RASENMAEHER - German for lawnmower; an infantry joke. So if you encounter a RASENMAEHER note that it means Deploy App.

The core rmapi

At the centre of the system is the core rmapi — the RASENMAEHER API. This is the rmapi service/container running the rasenmaeher_api application from the repo pvarki/python-rasenmaeher-api.

The core rmapi:

  • Owns the main user CRUD (create, approve, promote, demote, delete) and the identity that ties everything together.
  • Drives the Deploy App operations (invite codes, user approval, admin management).
  • Is the point of integration: every product integration registers with it, and it calls each integration over mTLS when a user changes.

For example, the first admin invite code is minted by the core rmapi:
docker compose exec -it rmapi /bin/bash -c "rasenmaeher_api addcode"

Product integration APIs

A product integration API (also called a product-rm integration API) is the small service you build to plug a product into Deploy App. It registers with / is driven by the core rmapi: when a user is created, promoted, demoted, or deleted, the core rmapi calls the integration's user-lifecycle endpoints over mTLS, and the integration reflects that change into its product.

Examples that ship with the stack:

  • pvarki/python-matrix-rmapi — Matrix / Synapse chat.
  • pvarki/python-tak-rmapi — TAK (situational awareness).
  • pvarki/python-mediamtx-rmmtxauthz — MediaMTX video streaming.

To build your own, start from pvarki/python-integration-template, the Copier scaffold for a new integration. See the Build an Integration book for the full workflow.

Two deployment stacks

Presently Deploy App can be deployed two different ways, and these docs treat them as genuinely different systems:

  • Legacy — Docker Compose (pvarki/docker-rasenmaeher-integration). The production stack today. It uses a bootstrap service called miniwerk (Let's Encrypt certificates, subdomains, the MW_PRODUCTS list) and CFSSL as the internal CA. Components are pulled in as git submodules.
  • New — Kubernetes (pvarki/opendefence-platform). An alpha, modular direction. It drops the old bootstrap service miniwerk and CFSSL as a CA: deployment is described with Kustomize (base/ + overlays/<env>) applied via task/kubectl, and certificates/trust come from cert-manager, trust-manager, and the opendefense-pki CA. Supporting pieces run as Kubernetes operators.

See Choose your platform: legacy Docker vs Kubernetes to decide which one applies to you, and note that each documentation page carries a platform toggle (shared / legacy / k8s).

Where to go next

  • Operate — run Deploy App: stand up the stack, manage users and admins, day-2 operations and audit logging.
  • Develop Deploy App — work on the Deploy App platform itself (the compose stack or the Kubernetes manifests).
  • Build an Integration — add a new product using a product integration API.
  • Contribute to Project — coding standards, CI, and community rules (see the Community & Standards page there).

For shared vocabulary, see the Glossary. For a conceptual map of the moving parts, see Architecture orientation.
